output.title: Focus blocks come after the workflow decision
output.body:
Before you protect a focus block, decide what is actually stealing the time.

For a small business owner, the useful question is not whether AI sounds clever. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If the work changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. If it repeats in a pattern, it may be a workflow worth measuring.

A simple test is enough: does the task follow a pattern, repeat weekly, and have a clear input and output? If yes, note it for a week before you decide whether to keep it manual, hand it to a hire, or scope it for automation. No spreadsheet heroics required; a week of plain notes usually tells you more than guesswork does.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and only then define a pilot scope if it does. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. The customer still keeps final approval.

The first move is simple: name the one task, time how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it really repeats before you protect the block. That is usually the part people skip.
